title: Great Lent
hook: Eastern Lent begins on Clean Monday with stricter fasting

segments.voice: Yesterday, theosis: being drawn into God's life by grace, like iron glowing in a fire and still iron. Your line was made sharers. What did you share? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

Sunday evening, in a Byzantine Catholic church. Vespers has just ended, and something unusual happens. The priest steps down and bows to the people, and asks their forgiveness. Then the people line up, and one by one they bow to each other. Forgive me, a sinner. God forgives, the other answers. A teenager bows to her grandmother. Two men who haven't spoken in months end up face to face in the line. The next morning, there are no ashes, no Wednesday. Lent has simply begun, on a Monday, and it has a name that sounds like a fresh sheet of paper. Today, the season that starts with everybody asking forgiveness.
screen: `THE PRIEST BOWS TO THE PEOPLE.` → `FORGIVE ME. GOD FORGIVES.` → `LENT BEGINS ON A MONDAY.`

segments.voice: The name sets the tone. Eastern Christians call it Great Lent, and its first day Clean Monday. The idea is in Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wash yourselves, be clean." Not a scrubbed kitchen, though some families do clean house. A clean heart, after a night of forgiving and being forgiven. Next, the fast. Western Catholics today fast on a few set days of Lent and abstain from meat on its Fridays. The traditional Byzantine fast asks more: through the whole season, meat and dairy are set aside, and on Clean Monday some people eat very little at all. Eastern Catholic churches differ in how strictly they keep it now, and people are often given gentler rules for health or work. Eastern teachers say the point was never the menu. It's freedom: a body that learns it can say no to a craving can learn to say yes to God. Then the prayer that marks the season. In Byzantine churches, a short prayer attributed to Saint Ephrem the Syrian is said on weekdays of Lent with deep bows. It asks God to take away laziness, discouragement, the lust for power and idle talk, and to give chastity, humility, patience and love, and the grace to see one's own faults and not judge a brother. Last, Jesus's own instruction about fasting, which East and West both read: "But thou, when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face." No sour face. No show. Fasting done cleanly, from Clean Monday on, all the way to the feast at the end.
screen: `WASH YOURSELVES, BE CLEAN.` · `A LONGER, STRICTER FAST.` · `THE PRAYER OF SAINT EPHREM.` · `NO SOUR FACE, NO SHOW.` · then, large: `ANOINT THY HEAD, AND WASH THY FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to simplify one meal. Settle, and breathe. Think of your next meal, or tomorrow's. What would it look like plainer? Bread and soup. Rice and beans. One dish instead of three. No dessert. Picture yourself eating it slowly, without the phone. Then think of what that small freedom might make room for: an apology, a phone call, a moment of prayer, money you could give away. If you pray, you can offer the plain meal for someone who has too little. If you don't, let it be a small act of attention. The bell holds the time.
Great Lent. The Eastern season of fasting before Pascha, beginning on Clean Monday, after a Sunday of mutual forgiveness, with a longer and stricter fast. Today's word.
Your line: clean monday. Today, eat one meal plainer than usual, and if someone comes to mind whom you need to ask forgiveness of, don't wait for Lent. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: In the Byzantine Catholic churches, Great Lent begins on Clean Monday after Forgiveness Sunday vespers, where people ask one another's forgiveness; the traditional fast sets aside meat and dairy, and the Prayer of Saint Ephrem is said with prostrations on Lenten weekdays.
